classification.difficultyReason: Construct the ordered-pair array, identify outcomes with sum at least 10 and their overlap with a first throw of 4, then compare P(A∩B) with P(A)P(B). Distinguishing independence from mutual exclusivity requires separate tests, but both follow taught methods and the array requested in part a scaffolds the counting.

content.prompt: Consider rolling a die on two separate occasions. Define event $A$ as ‘rolling a 4 on the first throw’ and event $B$ as ‘rolling at least 10 as the sum of the two numbers shown’.

children.label: a
children.prompt: Create a table (array) showing the sample space of a die rolled twice.

inlines.text: Rows show the first throw; columns show the second throw.
Record each outcome as (first throw, second throw). Each of the six first-throw results pairs with all six second-throw results, giving 36 equally likely outcomes.

children.label: b
children.prompt: Determine whether events $A$ and $B$ are independent.

answer.worked:
There are 36 equally likely ordered pairs. Event $A$ contains the six pairs with first entry 4.

$$B=\{(4,6),(5,5),(5,6),(6,4),(6,5),(6,6)\}.$$

$$A\cap B=\{(4,6)\}.$$

$$\begin{align*}P(A)&=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16,\\P(B)&=\frac{6}{36}=\frac16,\\P(A\cap B)&=\frac1{36},\\P(A)P(B)&=\frac16\times\frac16=\frac1{36}.\end{align*}$$

Since $P(A\cap B)=P(A)P(B)$, events $A$ and $B$ are independent.

children.label: c
children.prompt: Determine whether events $A$ and $B$ are mutually exclusive.

answer.worked:
$$A\cap B=\{(4,6)\},\qquad P(A\cap B)=\frac1{36}\ne0.$$

Both events can occur together, so $A$ and $B$ are not mutually exclusive.
